entries.lesson_core_move: Represent a continuous-time signal as shifted impulse components whose locations and weights encode its time-domain values for later LTI impulse-response analysis.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Representing Signals with Shifted Impulses
sections.learning_goal: State how a shifted impulse component records one time location and one signal value so a signal can be represented as components for later LTI analysis.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; use compact delta notation and short value lists instead of plots.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Introduce a shifted impulse component a delta(t - t0) as a symbolic marker for the signal value a at time t0.
tutorial_outline.base_case: A single nonzero signal value x(2) = 3 represented by 3 delta(t - 2).
paragraph_plan: Remind the learner that shifted impulses have locations and that later LTI analysis will use impulse components as building blocks.
Define a delta(t - t0) as an impulse located at t0 with weight a.
Separate the two pieces of information: the shift gives the time location and the multiplier gives the encoded signal value.
Explain that a finite list of signal values can be encoded by adding one shifted impulse component for each listed value.
Preview that later lessons use these components to build system outputs, while this lesson only reads and writes the components.
display_math_plan: Show the general component a delta(t - t0).
Show a two-component representation such as 3 delta(t - 2) - delta(t + 1).

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the introduction focused on the location-weight encoding convention; do not introduce convolution or output-response formulas yet.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Time Location of a Shifted Impulse
sections.learning_goal: Identify the time location encoded by the shift in a single impulse expression.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the task is to read the shift from symbolic delta notation.

question_policy.answer_format: One time location, written as t = value.
question_policy.practice_question_model: For the shifted impulse delta(t - 4), what time location does the impulse mark?
distractor_plan: Use a sign-reversal option such as t = -4.
Include t = 0 to catch treating every impulse as unshifted.
Include an option that repeats the shift expression instead of the location.
Include a nearby integer location to catch superficial pattern matching.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Identify the time location of the shifted impulse delta(t - 4).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that delta(t - 4) is located at t = 4.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: First active use after the tutorial; isolate the location cue before introducing non-unit weights.
solution_step_plan: Match the expression to the pattern delta(t - t0).
Read t0 = 4 from the shift.
State that the impulse is located at t = 4.
practice_variation_axes: Use positive and negative integer locations.
Use both delta(t - a) and delta(t + a) forms.
Occasionally use simple fractional locations once integer shifts are clear.

sections.handoff_notes: Make the sign convention explicit: delta(t + a) is located at t = -a.

sections.section_title: Interpreting the Weight on a Shifted Impulse
sections.learning_goal: Distinguish the impulse weight from the impulse location in a weighted shifted-impulse expression.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the task is to parse coefficient and shift from notation.

question_policy.practice_question_model: In 5 delta(t + 1), what are the impulse weight and time location?
distractor_plan: Swap the weight and location.
Reverse the sign of the location.
Reverse the sign of the weight.
Treat the coefficient as a time shift instead of a multiplier.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: In -3 delta(t - 2), identify the impulse weight and the time location.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the weight is -3 and the impulse is located at t = 2.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Add the coefficient as a second piece of information while keeping a single shifted impulse.
solution_step_plan: Identify the multiplier outside delta as the weight.
Match the shifted impulse to delta(t - t0).
Read the time location from the shift.
Report the weight and location as separate data.
practice_variation_axes: Use positive and negative weights.
Use positive, negative, and zero locations.
Vary whether the shift is written with plus or minus notation.

sections.handoff_notes: Do not describe the weight as area unless it is immediately tied back to the encoded signal value; the section's purpose is notation parsing.

sections.section_title: Encoding One Signal Value with a Shifted Impulse
sections.learning_goal: Write the shifted-impulse component that encodes one specified signal value at one specified time.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; give the signal value as text or compact notation such as x(3) = -2.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Write the shifted-impulse component that encodes x(2) = 5.
distractor_plan: Expected errors include reversing the shift sign.
Expected errors include writing the time location as the coefficient.
Expected errors include omitting the coefficient when the value is not 1.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Write the shifted-impulse component that encodes x(3) = -2.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Produce -2 delta(t - 3) from the given signal value and time location.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Reverse the direction of the task: generate the component from a value-location pair instead of reading the pair from a component.
solution_step_plan: Identify the target time t0 from x(t0).
Use the signal value as the coefficient.
Write delta(t - t0) with the correct shift sign.
Combine the coefficient and shifted impulse into one component.
practice_variation_axes: Use positive and negative signal values.
Use positive, negative, and zero time locations.
Use integer values first, then simple fractions only if notation remains clear.

sections.handoff_notes: The answer should be an expression, not an explanation; use free response so learners must generate the notation.

sections.section_title: Encoding Multiple Signal Values with Shifted Impulses
sections.learning_goal: Write a sum of shifted impulse components that encodes multiple specified signal values.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; present the data as a short list or table of time-value pairs.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Write a shifted-impulse representation for x(-1) = 2, x(0) = -3, and x(4) = 1.
distractor_plan: Expected errors include reversing one or more shift signs.
Expected errors include dropping a negative coefficient.
Expected errors include omitting the delta(t) term for a value at t = 0.
Expected errors include combining unlike impulse locations into one coefficient.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Write a shifted-impulse representation for x(-1) = 2, x(0) = 3, and x(4) = -1.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Produce 2 delta(t + 1) + 3 delta(t) - delta(t - 4) by assigning one component to each listed value.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extend from one value-location pair to a controlled sum of three independent components.
solution_step_plan: List each time-value pair separately.
Convert each pair into one shifted impulse component.
Check the shift sign for negative, zero, and positive time locations.
Add the components into one representation.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the number of listed nonzero values from two to four.
Include a mix of negative, zero, and positive locations.
Include both positive and negative weights.
Keep values sparse enough that the task tests encoding, not algebraic simplification.

sections.handoff_notes: Use subgoal labels around converting each pair and assembling the sum; do not advance to integrals or continuous sifting yet.

sections.section_title: Reading a Shifted-Impulse Representation for LTI Analysis
sections.learning_goal: Extract the component weights and locations from a shifted-impulse representation as the data that will later drive LTI impulse-response analysis.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the representation itself is the data for the task.

question_policy.answer_format: A component list giving each weight and time location.
question_policy.practice_question_model: For x(t) = 4 delta(t - 3) - delta(t + 2), which component list correctly records the weights and locations for later LTI analysis?
distractor_plan: Reverse one or both location signs.
Drop the negative sign on a weight.
Swap a coefficient with a time location.
Omit one component from the list.
State a response formula instead of the input component data.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Read the component list in x(t) = 2 delta(t + 1) - 3 delta(t - 2) for later LTI analysis.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Identify the components as weight 2 at t = -1 and weight -3 at t = 2 without computing an output response.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Move from writing a representation to reading a complete representation as the input-component data needed before applying an impulse response.
solution_step_plan: Separate the representation into individual shifted-impulse terms.
For each term, record the coefficient as the weight.
For each term, record the shift location using the delta(t - t0) convention.
State the component list in a format that can later be paired with h(t).
practice_variation_axes: Use two or three components.
Mix plus-form and minus-form shifts.
Include one negative weight.
Avoid asking for the output y(t) until the later LTI-response lessons.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the forward reference to LTI systems limited to identifying input components; do not derive convolution, sifting integrals, or shifted impulse responses in this lesson.

entries.lesson_core_move: Express a continuous-time signal as a continuum of shifted impulses using the sifting identity \(x(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)\delta(t-\tau)\,d\tau\).

sections.section_title: Introduction to Continuous-Time Sifting Representation
sections.learning_goal: State the continuous-time sifting identity and interpret it as reconstructing a signal from a continuum of shifted impulses.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the tutorial should use compact notation and verbal interpretation rather than a decorative signal plot.

question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Define the sifting representation and make clear that the integration variable \(\tau\) indexes shifted impulses whose weights come from \(x(\tau)\).
tutorial_outline.base_case: Use a generic continuous-time signal \(x(t)\) and show that integrating \(x(\tau)\delta(t-\tau)\) over all \(\tau\) returns \(x(t)\).
paragraph_plan: Remind the learner that a shifted impulse \(\delta(t-\tau)\) is located at the value selected by \(\tau\) and can pick out a signal value through the sifting property.
State the sifting identity and identify the roles of \(t\), \(\tau\), \(x(\tau)\), \(\delta(t-\tau)\), and \(d\tau\).
Explain that the integral is a continuous superposition of shifted impulses weighted by the signal values, not an ordinary area accumulation over nonzero-width pulses.
Connect the representation to the module flow by noting that decomposing an input into shifted impulses prepares the input for later LTI-system response construction.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: not-applicable
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: not-applicable
example_outline.variation_from_previous: not-applicable

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the tutorial concise and first-pass: define the identity, interpret each symbol, and avoid deriving convolution or introducing impulse response notation.

sections.section_title: Evaluating a Sifting Integral at a Fixed Time
sections.learning_goal: Evaluate a sifting integral by identifying the impulse-selected value of the integration variable and substituting that value into the weighting expression.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the selected value and resulting evaluation are fully determined by the symbolic delta expression.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Evaluate \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(2\tau-1)\delta(4-\tau)\,d\tau\).

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Evaluate \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(\tau^2+1)\delta(3-\tau)\,d\tau\).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the impulse selects \(\tau=3\), so the integral equals \(3^2+1=10\).
example_outline.variation_from_previous: First active use of the sifting identity at a fixed numeric time rather than as a general reconstruction formula.
solution_step_plan: Identify the weighting expression as \(f(\tau)=\tau^2+1\).
Identify the selected value \(\tau=3\) from the shifted impulse.
Evaluate the weighting expression at the selected value.
State the final scalar value of the integral.
practice_variation_axes: Change the selected time to another integer.
Use a different low-degree polynomial or affine weighting expression.
Keep the limits infinite so the focus remains on sifting rather than support restriction.

sections.handoff_notes: The worked example should model the substitution as the main move; do not introduce sign subtleties beyond recognizing that \(\delta(3-\tau)\) selects \(\tau=3\).

sections.section_title: Reconstructing x(t) with delta(t-tau)
sections.learning_goal: Simplify a symbolic sifting integral with free variable \(t\) by replacing \(\tau\) with \(t\) in the signal expression.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the task is recognizing the symbolic replacement induced by \(\delta(t-\tau)\).

question_policy.practice_question_model: Simplify \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}(\tau+1)u(\tau-1)\delta(t-\tau)\,d\tau\).

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Simplify \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-2\tau}u(\tau)\delta(t-\tau)\,d\tau\).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the integral reconstructs \(e^{-2t}u(t)\) by replacing every \(\tau\) in the weighting expression with \(t\).
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Keeps the same sifting move but changes the selected value from a fixed number to the symbolic time variable \(t\).
solution_step_plan: Identify the coefficient multiplying the impulse as the signal expression in \(\tau\).
Use \(\delta(t-\tau)\) to select the value \(\tau=t\).
Replace each occurrence of \(\tau\) in the coefficient with \(t\).
State the reconstructed signal expression.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the exponential, polynomial, or step-modulated expression multiplying the impulse.
Require replacement of \(\tau\) in more than one factor.
Keep the delta term in the form \(\delta(t-\tau)\) to reinforce the reconstruction identity.

sections.handoff_notes: Emphasize variable roles: \(\tau\) is integrated out, while \(t\) remains in the reconstructed signal.

sections.section_title: Writing a Signal as a Sifting Integral
sections.learning_goal: Convert a given signal expression \(x(t)\) into its continuous-time sifting integral by writing the weight as \(x(\tau)\).

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; the conversion is between two symbolic forms of the same signal.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Write \(x(t)=e^{-3t}u(t)\) as a continuous-time sifting integral.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Write \(x(t)=\cos(2t)u(t)\) as a continuous-time sifting integral.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that \(x(t)\) can be written as \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\cos(2\tau)u(\tau)\delta(t-\tau)\,d\tau\).
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Reverses the previous section's simplification task: instead of reducing a sifting integral to \(x(t)\), the learner builds the sifting integral from \(x(t)\).
solution_step_plan: Start from the general identity \(x(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)\delta(t-\tau)\,d\tau\).
Rewrite the given signal expression with \(\tau\) replacing \(t\) to form \(x(\tau)\).
Place \(x(\tau)\) as the weight multiplying \(\delta(t-\tau)\).
Use infinite limits because no support restriction has been requested.
practice_variation_axes: Vary the signal expression while keeping it compact.
Include one factor that depends on time so the learner must replace \(t\) by \(\tau\).
Keep the requested form as an all-time sifting integral before adding support-restricted limits later.

sections.handoff_notes: The example writer should make the direction change explicit: the learner is constructing the representation, not evaluating it.

sections.section_title: Restricting the Sifting Integral to the Signal Support
sections.learning_goal: Write a sifting representation with finite integration limits by using the interval on which the signal is nonzero.

image_policy.image_generation_notes: No image needed; provide the support interval in text or symbolic notation rather than requiring graph inspection.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Write the signal \(x(t)=t+1\) for \(-1\le t\le 2\), and \(x(t)=0\) otherwise, as a sifting integral with limits restricted to its support.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Write the signal \(x(t)=2t\) for \(0\le t\le 3\), and \(x(t)=0\) otherwise, as a sifting integral with limits restricted to its support.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that only the support interval contributes, giving \(x(t)=\int_{0}^{3}2\tau\delta(t-\tau)\,d\tau\).
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds one wrinkle to the all-time representation by replacing infinite limits with the signal's nonzero support interval.
solution_step_plan: Identify the support interval from the signal description.
Rewrite the nonzero signal formula with \(\tau\) replacing \(t\).
Use the support interval as the lower and upper limits of integration.
Multiply by \(\delta(t-\tau)\) and state the restricted sifting integral.
practice_variation_axes: Change the support interval endpoints.
Change the simple formula used on the support.
Include signals described as zero outside the interval so no graph is needed.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep support restriction as the only new feature; do not ask the learner to infer support from a graph or to compute an LTI-system output.

entries.lesson_core_move: Assign the weight \(x(\tau)\) to each shifted impulse \(\delta(t-\tau)\) in the continuous-time decomposition so the impulse continuum can be passed through an LTI system by superposition.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Weighted Impulse Decomposition
sections.learning_goal: Explain that each shifted impulse \(\delta(t-\tau)\) in the continuous-time decomposition carries the signal value \(x(\tau)\) as its weight.

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Make the weighting rule explicit: the impulse location \(\tau\) selects a shifted impulse, the signal value \(x(\tau)\) supplies its coefficient, and the continuum of weighted impulses reconstructs \(x(t)\).
tutorial_outline.base_case: If \(x(2)=5\), then the shifted impulse at \(\tau=2\) is weighted by 5, giving the component \(5\delta(t-2)\).
paragraph_plan: Connect back to the sifting representation by stating that reconstruction requires one shifted impulse for each possible value of \(\tau\).
State the local rule in words: the impulse at location \(\tau\) receives the signal value at that same location as its weight.
Introduce the component notation \(x(\tau_0)\delta(t-\tau_0)\) for a single selected location.
Show the full integral as the continuum version of adding all weighted shifted impulses.
Preview the structural reason this matters: the weighted impulse continuum can later be passed through an LTI system by superposition, but do not derive the output formula yet.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: not-applicable
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: not-applicable
example_outline.variation_from_previous: not-applicable

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the tutorial concise and focused on the weighting rule. Avoid convolution, system output, or any new LTI response formula beyond the superposition motivation.

sections.section_title: Matching a Shifted Impulse to Its Signal Value
sections.learning_goal: Identify the scalar weight attached to a specified shifted impulse by evaluating the signal at the impulse location.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Given \(x(\tau)=\tau^2-1\), what weight matches the shifted impulse \(\delta(t-2)\)?

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Given \(x(\tau)=2\tau+1\), match the shifted impulse \(\delta(t-3)\) to its signal value weight.
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that \(\delta(t-3)\) corresponds to \(\tau=3\), then evaluate \(x(3)=7\) and name 7 as the weight.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This is the first active use of the tutorial rule at a single specified impulse location.
solution_step_plan: Read the impulse location from the expression \(\delta(t-3)\).
Substitute that location into the signal expression.
State the resulting signal value as the impulse weight, without writing the full weighted component yet.
practice_variation_axes: Change the signal expression while keeping evaluation arithmetic simple.
Change the impulse location to a positive integer or zero.
Use notation that forces the learner to distinguish \(t\) from the indexing variable \(\tau\).

sections.handoff_notes: This section should isolate the matching move only: locate \(\tau_0\), evaluate \(x(\tau_0)\), and stop at the scalar weight.

sections.section_title: Writing a Single Weighted Impulse Component
sections.learning_goal: Write one complete weighted impulse component by combining the evaluated signal weight with the correct shifted impulse.

question_policy.practice_question_model: For \(x(\tau)=\tau+5\), write the weighted impulse component located at \(\tau=-2\).

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For a signal with \(x(\tau)=4-\tau\), write the weighted impulse component located at \(\tau=1\).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Evaluate \(x(1)=3\) and write the component as \(3\delta(t-1)\).
example_outline.variation_from_previous: The learner now writes the full weighted impulse expression instead of only identifying the scalar weight.
solution_step_plan: Identify the requested impulse location \(\tau_0\).
Evaluate the signal value \(x(\tau_0)\).
Attach that value as the coefficient of the shifted impulse \(\delta(t-\tau_0)\).
Check the sign inside the impulse shift against the location.
practice_variation_axes: Use positive, zero, or negative impulse locations.
Vary whether the signal expression is constant, affine, or a simple polynomial.
Require the answer as a single symbolic component rather than a verbal description.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this as a controlled extension from scalar matching to expression writing; do not introduce sums of components until the next section.

sections.section_title: Writing Several Weighted Impulse Components
sections.learning_goal: Write a finite collection of weighted impulse components by applying the same evaluation-and-attach rule at several impulse locations.

question_policy.answer_format: finite sum or ordered list of weighted impulse components
question_policy.practice_question_model: Using \(x(\tau)=2\tau+1\), write the weighted impulse components at \(\tau=0\), \(\tau=1\), and \(\tau=3\).

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Using \(x(\tau)=\tau+3\), write the weighted impulse components at \(\tau=0\), \(\tau=1\), and \(\tau=2\).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Evaluate the three signal values and write the corresponding components as \(3\delta(t)\), \(4\delta(t-1)\), and \(5\delta(t-2)\).
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This repeats the single-component move several times and organizes the results as a small finite decomposition.
solution_step_plan: List the requested locations in order.
Evaluate \(x(\tau)\) at each location.
Pair each weight with the shifted impulse centered at the same location.
Write the components as a finite sum or clearly ordered list.
practice_variation_axes: Change the number of listed locations between two and four.
Use simple signal expressions that keep arithmetic subordinate to the decomposition move.
Vary whether the locations include zero while keeping all weights nonnegative before the next section.

sections.handoff_notes: The example should make the repeated subgoal structure visible so later practice builds fluency with location-value-component matching.

sections.section_title: Handling Zero and Negative Impulse Weights
sections.learning_goal: Correctly write weighted impulse components when evaluating the signal produces zero or negative weights.

question_policy.answer_format: finite sum or ordered list of weighted impulse components, with zero components omitted or explicitly marked as zero
question_policy.practice_question_model: Using \(x(\tau)=2-\tau\), write the weighted impulse components at \(\tau=0\), \(\tau=2\), and \(\tau=4\).

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Using \(x(\tau)=\tau-1\), write the weighted impulse components at \(\tau=0\), \(\tau=1\), and \(\tau=3\).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the weights are \(-1\), 0, and 2, then write the nonzero components as \(-\delta(t)\) and \(2\delta(t-3)\), noting that the zero-weight component contributes nothing.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This keeps the multi-component structure but adds the sign and zero-weight cases that affect how components are written.
solution_step_plan: Evaluate the signal at each listed location.
Mark any zero weight as a component that contributes nothing.
Attach negative weights as negative coefficients rather than changing the impulse location.
Write the resulting expression, either omitting the zero component or explicitly showing it as zero.
practice_variation_axes: Move which listed location produces the zero weight.
Include one negative weight and at least one positive weight.
Vary whether the final answer is requested as a sum or an ordered component list.

sections.handoff_notes: Emphasize that coefficient sign and impulse location are separate: a negative weight changes the coefficient, not the shift. This closes the lesson without passing components through an LTI system.

entries.lesson_title: From Impulse Decomposition to System Output
entries.lesson_core_move: Convert a weighted shifted-impulse input decomposition into the corresponding LTI output by replacing each shifted impulse with the matching shifted, scaled impulse response and superposing the responses.

sections.section_title: Introduction to From Impulse Decomposition to System Output
sections.learning_goal: State the rule that a weighted shifted-impulse input component produces the matching shifted, scaled impulse response in an LTI system, and show how finite impulse decompositions turn into output sums.

question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Make explicit that an LTI system maps each input component a_k delta(t - t_k) to a_k h(t - t_k), then adds the component responses by superposition.
tutorial_outline.base_case: A finite decomposition with two weighted shifted impulses, such as x(t) = 2 delta(t - 1) - delta(t - 3).
paragraph_plan: Recall that h(t) is the output to delta(t), so time invariance sends delta(t - t_k) to h(t - t_k).
Recall that homogeneity sends a_k delta(t - t_k) to a_k h(t - t_k).
State that linearity adds the component responses when the input is a finite sum of weighted shifted impulses.
Preview the output rule y(t) = sum_k a_k h(t - t_k) for finite impulse decompositions.
display_math_plan: Show a_k delta(t - t_k) maps to a_k h(t - t_k).
Show x(t) = sum_k a_k delta(t - t_k) maps to y(t) = sum_k a_k h(t - t_k).

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this as direct instruction only; do not derive convolution yet or introduce integral notation beyond the finite-sum idea.

sections.section_title: Output from a Single Shifted Impulse
sections.learning_goal: Convert a single shifted impulse input into the corresponding shifted impulse response.

question_policy.answer_format: An expression for y(t) as one shifted copy of h(t).
question_policy.practice_question_model: An LTI system has impulse response h(t). Find the output when x(t) = delta(t + 3).
distractor_plan: Watch for reversing the sign of the shift, such as writing h(t - 3) for delta(t + 3).
Watch for leaving the output as delta notation instead of replacing the impulse with h.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: An LTI system has impulse response h(t). Find the output when x(t) = delta(t - 2).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that a shift in the impulse input produces the same shift in the impulse response, so y(t) = h(t - 2).
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Uses the simplest nonzero input component: one shifted impulse with unit weight.
solution_step_plan: Identify the shift location in delta(t - 2).
Use time invariance to replace delta(t - 2) with h(t - 2) at the output.
Write the final output as y(t) = h(t - 2).
practice_variation_axes: Change the shift value.
Use an advance such as delta(t + 1).
Use different notation for the shift parameter.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the worked example close to the shifted-impulse rule from the LTI setup; do not introduce scaling or multiple terms yet.

sections.section_title: Output from a Scaled Shifted Impulse
sections.learning_goal: Convert a scaled shifted impulse input into the corresponding scaled shifted impulse response.

question_policy.answer_format: An expression for y(t) as one scaled shifted copy of h(t).
question_policy.practice_question_model: An LTI system has impulse response h(t). Find the output when x(t) = -2 delta(t + 4).
distractor_plan: Watch for dropping the coefficient on the impulse response.
Watch for reversing the sign of the shift.
Watch for multiplying the time argument by the coefficient instead of scaling the response.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: An LTI system has impulse response h(t). Find the output when x(t) = 3 delta(t - 1).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the input weight multiplies the shifted impulse response, so y(t) = 3 h(t - 1).
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Adds one coefficient multiplying the shifted impulse.
solution_step_plan: Identify the shift and weight in 3 delta(t - 1).
Use time invariance to shift h(t) to h(t - 1).
Use homogeneity to carry the factor 3 to the output.
Write y(t) = 3 h(t - 1).
practice_variation_axes: Vary the positive coefficient.
Use a negative coefficient.
Use an advance or delay in the impulse argument.

sections.handoff_notes: Focus on coordinating the coefficient and the shift together; do not add multiple impulse terms yet.

sections.section_title: Output from a Finite Sum of Weighted Shifted Impulses
sections.learning_goal: Convert each term in a finite weighted shifted-impulse input into its matching output term and add the responses.

question_policy.answer_format: A finite sum expression for y(t) in shifted and scaled copies of h(t).
question_policy.practice_question_model: An LTI system has impulse response h(t). Find the output when x(t) = delta(t + 1) + 3 delta(t - 2) - 2 delta(t - 4).
distractor_plan: Watch for converting only one impulse term and leaving the others unchanged.
Watch for dropping negative signs or coefficients.
Watch for reversing one or more shift signs.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: An LTI system has impulse response h(t). Find the output when x(t) = 2 delta(t) - delta(t - 3) + 4 delta(t - 5).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Produce y(t) = 2 h(t) - h(t - 3) + 4 h(t - 5) by mapping each impulse term independently.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Extends from one scaled shifted impulse to several terms in a finite sum.
solution_step_plan: Separate the input into three weighted shifted impulse terms.
Map each delta(t - t_k) term to h(t - t_k).
Carry each coefficient to the corresponding response term.
Add the response terms to form y(t).
practice_variation_axes: Change the number of terms.
Include a zero shift.
Include negative weights.
Vary delay and advance locations.

sections.handoff_notes: Use finite sums only; save continuous integral notation for the following lesson.

sections.section_title: Superposing Responses from a Weighted Impulse Decomposition
sections.learning_goal: Apply the full finite-sum output rule to a compact weighted impulse decomposition and interpret the result as superposition of component responses.

question_policy.answer_format: A finite indexed-sum expansion for y(t) written in shifted and scaled copies of h(t).
question_policy.practice_question_model: An LTI system has impulse response h(t), and x(t) = sum_{k=1}^{3} a_k delta(t - t_k) with a_1 = 1, t_1 = -2, a_2 = 4, t_2 = 0, and a_3 = -3, t_3 = 3. Write y(t).
distractor_plan: Watch for using the index values as coefficients instead of reading a_k.
Watch for reversing signs when a listed shift t_k is negative.
Watch for omitting a term from the superposition.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: An LTI system has impulse response h(t), and x(t) = sum_{k=1}^{3} a_k delta(t - t_k) with a_1 = 2, t_1 = 0, a_2 = -1, t_2 = 2, and a_3 = 3, t_3 = 5. Write y(t).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Translate indexed weights and shifts into y(t) = 2 h(t) - h(t - 2) + 3 h(t - 5).
example_outline.variation_from_previous: Uses compact indexed decomposition data instead of writing each impulse term explicitly.
solution_step_plan: Read each coefficient a_k and shift t_k from the decomposition data.
Apply the rule a_k delta(t - t_k) maps to a_k h(t - t_k).
Write one response term for each k.
Superpose the terms into the final y(t).
practice_variation_axes: Vary indexed coefficients.
Vary the shift list.
Use a table of a_k and t_k values.
Include a negative coefficient or negative shift.

sections.handoff_notes: This should bridge to the next lesson by making the finite-sum pattern visible without deriving the convolution integral.

entries.lesson_core_move: Derive the continuous-time convolution integral \(y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau\) by applying linearity and time invariance to the weighted shifted-impulse decomposition of an input signal.

sections.section_title: Introduction to Deriving the Convolution Integral
sections.learning_goal: State how the weighted shifted-impulse representation of an input becomes an LTI output formed from weighted shifted impulse responses.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image; the construction is a symbolic derivation from the input representation to the output integral.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate a decorative system diagram or signal plot; keep the tutorial focused on the symbolic mapping.

question_policy.practice_question_model: not-applicable

tutorial_outline.direct_instruction_goal: Make explicit that the convolution integral is obtained by passing each weighted shifted impulse in the input decomposition through an LTI system and then superposing the resulting responses.
tutorial_outline.base_case: Begin with the known input decomposition \(x(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)\delta(t-\tau)\,d\tau\) and the known LTI mapping \(\delta(t-\tau)\mapsto h(t-\tau)\).
paragraph_plan: Recall that a continuous-time signal can be written as a continuum of weighted shifted impulses.
State that each shifted impulse component can be considered separately because the system is linear.
Use time invariance to explain why the response to \(\delta(t-\tau)\) is \(h(t-\tau)\).
Use linearity again to attach the weight \(x(\tau)\) to the shifted response.
Conclude that superposing all component responses over \(\tau\) gives the convolution integral.

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: not-applicable
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: not-applicable
example_outline.variation_from_previous: not-applicable

sections.handoff_notes: Keep this as construction guidance rather than a full proof; the tutorial should set up the one move that the examples will practice in increasingly complete symbolic form.

sections.section_title: Mapping a Shifted Impulse to a Shifted Impulse Response
sections.learning_goal: Apply time invariance to replace a shifted impulse input with the correspondingly shifted impulse response.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image; the learner only needs the symbolic shifted-impulse rule.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not request signal plots; the practice should vary shifts symbolically.

question_policy.practice_question_model: For an LTI system with impulse response \(h(t)\), determine the output produced by the input \(\delta(t-5)\).

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For an LTI system with impulse response \(h(t)\), determine the output produced by the input \(\delta(t-3)\).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the output is \(h(t-3)\) by applying time invariance to the impulse response.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This isolates the unweighted shifted-impulse mapping before adding input weights or superposition.
solution_step_plan: Recall that the response to \(\delta(t)\) is \(h(t)\).
Identify the shift amount in \(\delta(t-3)\).
Apply time invariance to shift the impulse response by the same amount.
State the component output as \(h(t-3)\).
practice_variation_axes: Change the positive shift value.
Use an advanced impulse such as \(\delta(t+2)\) once the sign convention is clear.
Ask for the output using only symbolic \(h\)-notation.

sections.handoff_notes: The example writer should emphasize the sign inside \(\delta(t-\tau)\) and \(h(t-\tau)\); avoid introducing the integral before the component mapping is secure.

sections.section_title: Applying the Input Weight to the Shifted Response
sections.learning_goal: Use linearity to carry the weight on a shifted impulse through to the corresponding shifted impulse response.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image; the section practices scalar weighting of symbolic shifted responses.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate visuals; the controlled wrinkle is the scalar multiplier.

question_policy.practice_question_model: For an LTI system with impulse response \(h(t)\), determine the output produced by the input \(-3\delta(t-1)\).

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For an LTI system with impulse response \(h(t)\), determine the output produced by the weighted shifted impulse \(4\delta(t-2)\).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the output is \(4h(t-2)\) by first mapping the shifted impulse and then applying the scalar weight.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This adds a scalar input weight to the shifted impulse while keeping a single impulse component.
solution_step_plan: Identify the unweighted shifted impulse \(\delta(t-2)\).
Map \(\delta(t-2)\) to \(h(t-2)\) by time invariance.
Apply homogeneity from linearity so the coefficient \(4\) multiplies the entire response.
State the weighted response as \(4h(t-2)\).
practice_variation_axes: Vary the scalar weight, including negative and fractional values.
Vary the impulse shift while preserving the same sign convention.
Use a symbolic weight such as \(a\) only after numeric weights are clear.

sections.handoff_notes: Prevent the common error of placing the weight inside the argument of \(h\); the weight multiplies the shifted response, not the time variable.

sections.section_title: Superposing Responses from the Impulse Decomposition
sections.learning_goal: Use linearity to add the outputs produced by multiple weighted shifted impulses as a finite bridge toward continuous superposition.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image; finite superposition can be represented with compact symbolic sums.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not use diagrams; keep attention on mapping each symbolic component and adding responses.

question_policy.answer_format: symbolic expression for \(y(t)\) in terms of shifted \(h\) terms
question_policy.practice_question_model: For an LTI system with impulse response \(h(t)\), write the output produced by the input \(3\delta(t+2)+5\delta(t-1)\).

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: For an LTI system with impulse response \(h(t)\), write the output produced by the input \(2\delta(t-1)-\delta(t-4)\).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that the output is \(2h(t-1)-h(t-4)\) by mapping each weighted shifted impulse and summing the component responses.
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This extends from one weighted shifted impulse to a finite sum of weighted shifted impulses.
solution_step_plan: Separate the input into the components \(2\delta(t-1)\) and \(-\delta(t-4)\).
Map each shifted impulse to its shifted impulse response.
Apply each scalar weight to the corresponding shifted response.
Add the component responses to form \(y(t)\).
practice_variation_axes: Vary the number of impulse terms from two to three.
Vary coefficients, including negative coefficients.
Vary shift signs while keeping the response notation in \(h(t-\tau)\) form.

sections.handoff_notes: Frame this as the finite-sum version of the convolution idea; do not jump to evaluating any actual convolution integral.

sections.section_title: Identifying the Continuous-Time Convolution Integral
sections.learning_goal: Convert the continuum of weighted shifted impulse responses into the convolution integral for the LTI system output.

image_policy.image_description_seed: No image; the final move is recognizing the symbolic continuum superposition.
image_policy.image_generation_notes: Do not generate overlap-area or flip-shift visuals; those belong to later convolution setup lessons.

question_policy.practice_question_model: Starting from \(x(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)\delta(t-\tau)\,d\tau\), write the output \(y(t)\) for an LTI system whose impulse response is \(h(t)\).

example_outline.worked_example_prompt: Starting from \(x(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)\delta(t-\tau)\,d\tau\), derive the expression for the output \(y(t)\) of an LTI system with impulse response \(h(t)\).
example_outline.worked_solution_goal: Show that each infinitesimal component \(x(\tau)\delta(t-\tau)\,d\tau\) contributes \(x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau\), so integrating all contributions gives \(y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau\).
example_outline.variation_from_previous: This replaces finite superposition with continuous superposition over all shifted impulse components.
solution_step_plan: Write the weighted shifted-impulse decomposition of \(x(t)\).
Map \(\delta(t-\tau)\) to \(h(t-\tau)\) using time invariance.
Carry the weight \(x(\tau)\) and infinitesimal width \(d\tau\) onto the component response.
Superpose all component responses by integrating over \(\tau\).
Identify the resulting expression as the continuous-time convolution integral.
practice_variation_axes: Ask for the full output integral from the input decomposition.
Ask for the integrand before the final integral is written.
Vary whether the prompt provides the component response mapping or asks the learner to supply it.

sections.handoff_notes: Keep the endpoint as derivation and identification of the formula; leave interpretation of \(\tau\), holding \(t\) fixed, and flip-shift-multiply-integrate mechanics to the following 6.3 lessons.
